\chapter{El Animo}
\label{ch:es-animo}
\hlchaptermodality{443}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what is going on inside me: what hurts, what I care about, what I am struggling to do, and what I wish I had not done.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[doler]{doler — the pain does the acting}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-doler}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el dolor} and \textbf{la cabeza}. You have the noun for pain and the part of you that has it. Name the verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: doler}
\textbf{doler} — to hurt, to ache.

\emph{Me duele la cabeza} — I have a headache. \emph{Me duelen los pies} — my feet hurt. \emph{¿Le duele aquí?} — does it hurt here? That last one is what a doctor says, and it is worth having ready before you need it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it is built like gustar}]
Look at \emph{me duele la cabeza} and find the subject. It is not \emph{me}. \textbf{La cabeza} is the subject; the head is what does the hurting, and \emph{me} is the person it happens to.

That is the same machine as \textbf{gustar}, which you have had since early on.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{what is the subject} \\
\midrule
me gusta el pan & \textbf{el pan} \\
me duele la cabeza & \textbf{la cabeza} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the verb agrees with the body part, not with you: \emph{me duele la cabeza} but \emph{me \textbf{duelen} los pies}. Two feet, plural verb. This is the single most common mistake English speakers make with the word, because English puts the person in charge — \emph{I have a headache} — and Spanish does not.

Nothing new is being learned here. You already owned the pattern; this is a second verb that runs on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{dolēre}, to hurt. \textbf{el dolor} is its noun and you have had it for a long time; \textbf{doler} is the verb it was cut from.

The stem breaks under stress, exactly as \emph{dormir} and \emph{torcer} do: \emph{doler}, \emph{dolemos}, but \textbf{duele} and \textbf{duelen}. Same condition, same result — when the stress lands on the \textbf{o}, the \textbf{o} opens into \textbf{ue}.

English keeps \emph{dolēre} in \textbf{condolence}, hurting \emph{with} somebody, and in \textbf{doleful}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{doler}
  \item I have a headache
  \item my feet hurt — and check which word the verb agreed with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To hurt? (\textbf{Doler}.) My feet hurt? (\textbf{Me duelen los pies}.) Which verb is it built like? (\emph{\textbf{Gustar}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[interesar]{interesar — what lies between you and a thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-interesar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{interesante} and \textbf{estudiar}. Say \textbf{doler}. You can call a class interesting. Now say that it interests \emph{you}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: interesar}
\textbf{interesar} — to interest, to be of interest to somebody.

\emph{Me interesa la clase} — the class interests me, I am interested in it. \emph{No me interesa} — I am not interested, which is the ordinary way to decline an offer. \textbf{interesarse por} is to take an interest in: \emph{se interesó por mi salud}.

You already had \textbf{interesante}. This is the verb the adjective was made from, so the only new thing is what it does in a sentence.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same machine again}]
\emph{Me interesa el curso} has the same shape as \emph{me duele la cabeza}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{the subject} & \textbf{the person} \\
\midrule
me duele \textbf{la cabeza} & la cabeza & me \\
me interesa \textbf{la clase} & la clase & me \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The verb agrees with the thing, not with you — \emph{me interesan \textbf{las clases}}, plural. Once you have seen the pattern three times (\emph{gustar}, \emph{doler}, \emph{interesar}) it stops being a special case and becomes what this whole family of verbs does.

English turns them the other way round and needs an adjective to do it: \emph{I am interested}. Spanish keeps the thing in charge.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{inter esse} — \textbf{inter}, between, plus \textbf{esse}, to be. To \emph{interest} somebody was for a thing \textbf{to be between} them and something else: to be involved, to be at stake.

That older sense is still in \textbf{el interés} on a loan, which is what is at stake in the deal, and in English \textbf{interested party} — not a party that is curious, but one with something at stake.

So \emph{interesante} does not mean \textquotedblleft{}makes me curious\textquotedblright{} at root. It means \textbf{standing between}, involved, concerned. The curiosity sense came later and took over.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{interesar}
  \item the class interests me and I want to study it
  \item \emph{no me interesa}, and why it is a polite refusal
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To interest? (\textbf{Interesar}.) What do the two Latin pieces mean? (\textbf{Between} and \textbf{to be}.) Which verbs is it built like? (\emph{\textbf{Gustar}} and \emph{\textbf{doler}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acercarse]{acercarse — making it near}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-acercarse}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{cerca} and \textbf{lejos}. Say \textbf{interesar}. You can say where something is. Name the act of closing the gap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acercarse}
\textbf{acercar} — to bring something nearer. \textbf{acercarse} — to come closer yourself.

\emph{Acércate} — come here, come closer. \emph{Me acerqué a la ventana} — I went over to the window. \emph{Se acerca la fecha} — the date is getting close, which a Spanish speaker says about an exam or a deadline the way English says \emph{it's coming up}.

It takes \textbf{a}: \emph{acercarse \textbf{a} algo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a-} plus \textbf{cerca} plus the \textbf{-ar} ending, and every piece is one you own.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
a- & towards \\
cerc- & \textbf{cerca}, near \\
-ar & makes it a verb \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is Spanish building a verb out of a preposition, and it does it constantly: \emph{acercar} from \emph{cerca}, \emph{alejar} from \emph{lejos}, \emph{aclarar} from \emph{claro}. The pattern is \textbf{a-} plus a word plus \textbf{-ar}, meaning \emph{to make it that}.

Underneath, \emph{cerca} is Latin \textbf{circā}, around — the same root English has in \textbf{circa} on a date and in \textbf{circle}. Something near you was something \emph{round about} you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The reflexive is doing real work. \textbf{Acercar} something is an act with an object; \textbf{acercarse} turns it back on the subject.

But notice the third example above. \emph{Se acerca la fecha} — the date does not move, and nobody moves it. Spanish still uses the reflexive, because what it marks is not \emph{doing it to yourself} so much as \textbf{nobody else did it}: the change happened, and the sentence declines to name an agent.

That is the same reflexive you met on \emph{equivocarse}, where the mistake befalls the person. One form, one job: take the doer out.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{acercarse}
  \item come closer, you are too far away
  \item the date is getting close
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To come closer? (\textbf{Acercarse}.) Which word is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Cerca}}.) Which preposition follows? (\emph{\textbf{A}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[concentrarse]{concentrarse — gathered to a point}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-concentrarse}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el centro} and \textbf{el examen}. Say \textbf{acercarse}. The exam is getting close. Name what you have to do with your attention.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: concentrarse}
\textbf{concentrarse} — to concentrate.

\emph{No me puedo concentrar} — I cannot concentrate. \emph{Concéntrate en el examen} — concentrate on the exam. \textbf{la concentración} is both the mental state and, in a notice, a gathering of people in a square.

It takes \textbf{en}: \emph{concentrarse \textbf{en} algo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{con-} together, plus \textbf{centr-} from \textbf{el centro}, plus the verb ending. To concentrate is \textbf{to bring together to a centre}, and the reflexive says you are doing it to yourself.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
con- & together \\
centr- & \textbf{el centro} \\
-arse & to yourself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the third verb in this chapter built by putting a prefix and an ending on a word you already owned — \emph{acercarse} on \emph{cerca}, \emph{concentrarse} on \emph{centro}. Look for the bare word inside before you look anything up.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{El centro} is not originally about the middle of a town.

Greek \textbf{kéntron} was \textbf{a goad} — the spike used to drive cattle — and then the fixed point of a pair of compasses, the spike you press into the paper so the other leg can swing round it. Latin took it as \emph{centrum}, and the geometry sense is what survived.

So a centre is, at bottom, \textbf{the point that does not move while everything else turns around it}. That is a better picture than \textquotedblleft{}the middle\textquotedblright{}, and it explains \emph{concentrarse}: you are pulling a scattered mind in towards the one fixed point.

English has the same spike in \textbf{eccentric} — \emph{ek-}, out of, plus the centre. An eccentric wheel is one whose axle is off the fixed point, and an eccentric person is one whose life turns around a different one.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{concentrarse}
  \item the exam is getting close and I cannot concentrate
  \item what \emph{kéntron} meant before it meant a centre
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To concentrate? (\textbf{Concentrarse}.) Which preposition follows it? (\emph{\textbf{En}}.) What was a \emph{kéntron}? (\textbf{A goad, then the fixed point of a pair of compasses}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[arrepentirse]{arrepentirse — the verb that is not made of \emph{sentir}}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-arrepentirse}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{perdón}. Say \textbf{equivocarse}. You can admit a mistake and you can ask to be excused for it. Name the feeling that comes in between.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: arrepentirse}
\textbf{arrepentirse} — to regret, to be sorry for having done something.

\emph{Me arrepiento de haberlo dicho} — I regret having said it. \emph{No te vas a arrepentir} — you will not regret it, which is what somebody says to talk you into something.

It takes \textbf{de}, and it is always reflexive. There is no plain \emph{arrepentir}.

\textbf{Equivocarse} is the error; \textbf{arrepentirse} is what you feel about it afterwards.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the trap, and this chapter has earned it.

\textbf{arrepentirse} looks like \textbf{a-} plus \textbf{re-} plus \textbf{sentir}, with the \textbf{s} worn away. It is not. There is no \emph{sentir} in it at all.

The middle is Latin \textbf{paenitēre}, to cause regret — the verb behind English \textbf{penitent}, \textbf{penance} and \textbf{repent}. Spanish took \emph{repentirse} and put its familiar \textbf{a-} on the front.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it looks like} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
a- + re- + sentir & a- + re- + \textbf{paenitēre} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And the trap is doubled, because \textbf{it conjugates like \emph{sentir} too}: \emph{me arrepiento}, \emph{te arrepientes}, \emph{se arrepiente}, \emph{nos arrepentimos}. That is the \textbf{e$\to$ie} break, exactly as \emph{siento}, \emph{sientes}, \emph{siente}, \emph{sentimos}.

So the form misleads and the behaviour agrees with the form. Both are accidents of shape: any verb with a stressed \textbf{e} in its stem breaks that way, related or not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is the strongest case yet for the test you have been building.

\textbf{reír} wore a prefix it never had, and the test caught it: take \emph{re-} off and nothing stands. \textbf{arrepentirse} is harder, because if you take \emph{a-} and \emph{re-} off you get \emph{pentir}, which stands on nothing — and the fact that it looks like \emph{sentir} is the only reason you would have thought otherwise.

What that means in practice: a resemblance is not evidence. \emph{Concentrarse} really does contain \emph{centro}, and you can check it because \emph{centro} is a word. \emph{Sentir} is a word too, and \emph{arrepentirse} still does not contain it.

The honest position is the one worth keeping — take the word apart where the pieces are real, and when they are not, learn the word and let the history be what it is.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{arrepentirse}
  \item I regret having said it
  \item why the \emph{-pentir-} is not \emph{sentir}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To regret? (\textbf{Arrepentirse}.) Which preposition follows it? (\emph{\textbf{De}}.) Is \emph{sentir} inside it? (\textbf{No — \emph{paenitēre} is}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(doler, interesar, acercarse …]{(doler, interesar, acercarse, concentrarse, arrepentirse) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R443-repaso-animo}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{to hurt}, \emph{to interest}, \emph{to come closer}, \emph{to concentrate}, \emph{to regret}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: five new words, no new grammar}]
This chapter taught nothing you did not already have. It handed five words to two machines you owned.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the machine} & \textbf{where you got it} & \textbf{the new words} \\
\midrule
\textbf{the thing is the subject} & \emph{gustar} & doler, interesar \\
\textbf{the reflexive} & \emph{equivocarse} & acercarse, concentrarse, arrepentirse \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Me duele la cabeza} — the head hurts, and the verb agrees with the head. \emph{Me interesan las clases} — plural thing, plural verb. If you can catch yourself about to say \emph{yo duelo}, the machine is working.

That is the whole point of building on what came before, and it is worth noticing when it happens: the fifth verb on a pattern costs almost nothing, where the first one cost a lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item my head hurts and I cannot concentrate
  \item I regret having said it
  \item \emph{me duele} and \emph{me duelen}, and what decides between them
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now say what is going on inside you} — what hurts, what you care about, what you are struggling to do and what you wish you had not done. A reading paper asks that constantly, because most short texts about people are about exactly this.

You also have the sharpest case yet of a word that misleads. \textbf{Arrepentirse} looks like it is made of \emph{sentir} and behaves like it, and is not related to it at all. A resemblance is not evidence, and the check is whether the piece you think you see is a word in its own right that leaves something standing behind it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
My feet hurt? (\textbf{Me duelen los pies}.) To come closer? (\textbf{Acercarse}.) To concentrate on something? (\textbf{Concentrarse en algo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un mensaje antes del examen) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C443-sintesis-animo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{concentrarse} and \emph{acercarse}. Both are in the message you are about to read, and one of them is about a date rather than a person.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — de Marta}

\begin{quote}
Se \textbf{acerca} el examen y no me puedo \textbf{concentrar} en nada. Llevo dos días con dolor de cabeza: me \textbf{duele} por la mañana y se me pasa por la tarde. ¿Tú cómo lo llevas?
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — la respuesta}

\begin{quote}
Yo igual. Me \textbf{arrepiento} de no haber empezado en septiembre. Pero me \textbf{interesa} de verdad la asignatura, así que algo se me quedará. Nos vemos el jueves y lo repasamos juntos.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what is making Marta anxious
  \item when her headache comes and when it goes
  \item what the second writer regrets, and what she says in spite of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Four of the five verbs in those messages put the writer in the object, not the subject. \textbf{Se acerca} el examen, \textbf{me duele} la cabeza, \textbf{me interesa} la asignatura, \textbf{me arrepiento} — in every one, something else is doing the acting and the writer is on the receiving end.

That is not a coincidence of these two messages. It is how Spanish talks about inner states by default: the feeling arrives, the date approaches, the subject interests. English reaches for \emph{I am} plus an adjective — \emph{I am worried}, \emph{I am interested} — and puts the person in charge of a state they did not choose.

Neither is more accurate. But if you translate your English shape word for word you will produce \emph{estoy interesado en} where a Spanish speaker says \emph{me interesa}, and the sentence will be understood and will not sound like theirs.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Five sentences about a week before something difficult: say the date is getting close, say what hurts, say you cannot concentrate, say what you regret, and say what still interests you.

Then check yourself: did you write \emph{me interesa}, or did you reach for \emph{estoy interesado}?
\end{tcolorbox}
